o: Seeding with value v destroys all targets congruent to v modulo space (v, v+space, v+2space, …). So the number of targets destroyed when seeding with nums[i] equals the count of elements sharing nums[i] mod space. We want the maximum such count, and among seeds achieving it, the minimum seed value. In example 1 (space=2): remainders — 3,7,1,1,5 all ≡ 1 (five targets), 8 ≡ 0 (one) — best count 5, minimum seed 1. Grouping by remainder with a hash map solves this in O(n).
k: All targets destroyed by seed v share v mod space, so group by remainder.
Ties broken by the minimum actual value in the best group.

a.i: For each element record count per remainder and the minimum element seen per remainder. The answer is the minimum element among remainders with maximal count.
s: Build count and min-value maps keyed by num % space.
Return the minimum value over keys attaining it.
a.t: O(n) — single grouping pass plus a scan of distinct remainders

a.i: Sort elements by (num % space, num). Equal remainders become contiguous runs; scan runs tracking the best (count, min value) — ties resolve naturally because within a run the first element is the minimum, and comparing runs by count then first element gives the required tie-break.
s: Scan contiguous runs of equal remainder.
Track max count; on ties take the smaller first element of the run.

w: The hash-map solution is the interview favorite: O(n) and simple. Remember the seed itself must be an element of nums, and the tie-break is on the seed value, not the remainder. Values up to 1e9 pose no overflow issues for counts. Follow-up: if the machine could be re-seeded after each shot, the problem becomes a simulation rather than pure counting.
